transcript:
[00:00] Sophie Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Maya Patel: Maya here, hey.
[00:07] Jonah Lee: Jonah, infra.
[00:09] Priya Rao: Priya, SRE.
[00:12] Diego Martinez: Diego from Redwood, ready to dig in.
[00:20] Sophie Chen: Cool. We're planning a 60-ish minute deep dive. Diego will drive profiling outputs and we'll leave time for Q&A.
[02:10] Diego Martinez: Ok, high level first — we've seen two main runtime paths customers ask about: the TensorRT-LLM optimized kernels (sometimes we call it TRT-LLM) and vLLM-style fused kernels. Both have different sweet spots. TRT-LLM gets you better throughput on long sequences and mixed-precision kernels, vLLM tends to be better for moderate batch sizes with aggressive CPU+GPU scheduling.
[04:30] Maya Patel: Can you explain that in concrete perf numbers? Our prod target is p50 latency <120ms for 1k token responses, and peak throughput 500 requests/sec.
[05:02] Diego Martinez: Right — numbers vary by model, sequence length, and tokenization. For a 7B model on A100, TRT-LLM path with CUDA graphs + int8 quant gave ~20-30% throughput improvement over baseline at batch sizes >8, but cold-start latency higher unless you warm the CUDA graph. vLLM path was lower max throughput but better p50 at small batches due to continuous batching and lighter kernel-launch overhead.
[07:15] Jonah Lee: When you say CUDA graphs warm, do you mean warm per model shape? We have lots of dynamic lengths.
[07:42] Diego Martinez: Good question. CUDA graphs prefer stable execution graphs. If your sequence lengths vary a lot, you can either build multiple graphs for common length buckets (e.g., 128/512/1024) or fallback to dynamic kernel for the tail. Building too many graphs increases memory and compile time. We usually suggest 3-4 buckets covering 80-90% of traffic.
[09:30] Priya Rao: Any gotchas with KV cache memory growth? We saw OOMs during long chat sessions.
[09:55] Diego Martinez: KV cache growth is linear with sequence length and per-beam if you do beam search. Two mitigations: streaming eviction policies (truncate older keys) and pinned shared KV buffers for identical sessions. Also quantized KV (4-bit) reduces memory but has accuracy tradeoffs.
[11:40] Maya Patel: About quantization — how much quality drop with 8-bit vs 4-bit in your experience?
[12:05] Diego Martinez: For many instruction-tuned 7B/13B models, 8-bit (dynamic quant) is often near-lossless in ROUGE/EM equivalent tests; 4-bit can show modest regressions on nuanced reasoning prompts. Real answer depends on model and eval set — we run regression evals as part of Recommend in Redwood Optimize.
[14:00] Jonah Lee: We're leaning to on-prem VPC with HSM KMS for keys. Any differences in runtime behavior when you're in private network?
[14:22] Sophie Chen: From the runtime side not much changes; it's more about orchestration and network egress for model downloads. But for benchmarking, ensure your private cluster has the same NICs and RDMA config — inter-GPU comms impact kernel perf for large batches and tensor parallel sharding.
[16:05] Diego Martinez: Back to kernel selection — there are a couple of heuristics we use: 1) sequence length distribution, 2) batch size distribution, 3) cost SLO tradeoffs. We run a kernel sweep: compare cuBLAS/cudnn matmul vs fused GEMM kernels in TRT path, and measure KV cache copy vs mapped pointers. Often fused TRT kernels beat generic matmul for attention patterns when head dims allow it.
[18:45] Maya Patel: Is kernel selection automatic in Redwood or manual?
[19:02] Diego Martinez: We have an automatic kernel selector that runs lightweight microbenchmarks on cold deploy and chooses a profile, but customers can override. For certain regulated workloads customers lock kernels after validation.
[21:30] Priya Rao: We've got a hard SLO and can't accept p95 latency spikes during cold starts. How do you handle cold-starts with CUDA graphs?
[21:50] Diego Martinez: Two approaches: eager graph build at deploy time (costly but avoids runtime compilation) or deferred warm-up traffic routing (send a small synthetic load through new nodes). Redwood can do both; for Dedicated we recommend eager graph build in maintenance windows.
[24:10] Jonah Lee: We saw jitter with vLLM under autoscaling — sometimes latency increases before the cluster scales. Any recommended autoscaler config?
[24:35] Diego Martinez: Autoscaling for latency-sensitive workloads should use predictive scaling based on recent token/sec trends, not only CPU/GPU utilization. Also keep a small reserve pool of warm workers. Batching thresholds matter — if you set max_batch_delay too high you risk tail latency.
[26:20] Maya Patel: On the benchmarking side — what artifacts will you share? We want to reproduce.
[26:38] Diego Martinez: We'll share: profiler traces (nvprof / Nsight/TX), CUDA graph traces, kernel invocation tables, and a comparison CSV of p50/p90/p95 and throughput for TRT-LLM vs vLLM under your traffic shape. We'll also include the config used (batch sizes, quant flags, sequence buckets).
[29:05] Priya Rao: Any recommendations for model quantization workflow? We want to try int8 first.
[29:22] Diego Martinez: Start with post-training dynamic quant (8-bit) and run your eval prompts. If quality is acceptable, test more aggressive 4-bit or mixed-precision for KV cache. Watch out for calibration data — choose representative prompts.
[31:00] Maya Patel: In our internal tests, vLLM seemed to have better KV cache reuse for streaming sessions; is that expected?
[31:22] Diego Martinez: vLLM's design emphasizes long-lived session efficiency with shared KV and scheduler optimizations; that's why it shines for streaming chat. TRT-LLM prioritizes fused dense kernels which favor throughput on batched generation. So matches your observation.
[33:40] Jonah Lee: When you say shared KV buffers, is that safe multi-tenant? We plan to run multiple tenants with strict isolation.
[33:58] Diego Martinez: Isolation is critical — shared KV is for single-tenant or per-namespace. For multi-tenant we allocate separate KV pool per tenant and enforce RBAC at the runtime network level. On Dedicated you can bind GPU pools to account IDs for hard isolation.
[36:10] Priya Rao: Any pitfalls with CUDA graph memory leaks? We hit growing memory over days.
[36:30] Diego Martinez: Memory leaks usually come from not properly destroying graphs when you update models or forget to free temporary scratch buffers allocated at graph build. Also pinned host allocations that are not released. We recommend lifecycle hooks that rebuild graphs and free resources on deploy.
[38:50] Maya Patel: Let's talk about latency vs throughput tradeoffs — we can't sacrifice p95 for throughput.
[39:10] Diego Martinez: You can tier traffic: critical paths go to low-latency nodes with smaller batches and vLLM profiles; background bulk inference to TRT nodes with large batches and quantization. Redwood routing policies can split by route/model/priority.
[41:00] Jonah Lee: For A/B testing kernel changes, what's the safest rollout strategy?
[41:20] Diego Martinez: Canary on a small subset, compare metrics, and auto-roll back on regressions. Also pin test prompts for regression detection. We support shadow testing without impacting production responses.
[43:05] Priya Rao: Our security/compliance team needs network diagrams for VPC and HSM integration. Will you provide?
[43:20] Sophie Chen: Yes, we'll send the VPC architecture diagram, KMS/HSM integration notes, and the SOC2 packet — Sophie to own.
[44:45] Maya Patel: A quick question about tensor parallelism — sometimes TRT fused kernels don't play well with model parallel configs.
[45:10] Diego Martinez: Correct — TRT fused kernels assume certain sharding patterns; for aggressive tensor parallel you might prefer vLLM or tuned AllReduce paths. We usually benchmark both.
[47:30] Jonah Lee: If we do on-prem, what's the recommended interconnect? We currently have 100GbE with RoCE; is that ok?
[47:52] Diego Martinez: RoCE with RDMA is fine; NVLink/NVSwitch gives best intra-node throughput for large tensor parallel work. Ensure RoCE is properly configured with low latency and jumbo frames.
[50:00] Maya Patel: Timeline-wise, we want a pilot in Jan. Can Redwood run the bench on our staging cluster?
[50:20] Sophie Chen: Yes — next steps: Diego will define the bench script and profiler commands, Jonah will provision the cluster, Sophie will send security docs.
[52:05] Diego Martinez: I'll include the kernel sweep script — it's a Lua/Python harness that steps through GEMM variants and measures wall time and CUDA occupancy.
[53:30] Priya Rao: Any quick wins we can try now?
[53:45] Diego Martinez: Turn on eager CUDA graph build for the hottest buckets and reduce max_batch_delay to 8ms for critical routes; try int8 on a subset.
[55:10] Maya Patel: Great. Also can you include suggestions for log/tracing fields to detect KV cache pressure?
[55:30] Diego Martinez: We'll include log keys: kv_cache_bytes, kv_evictions, graph_build_time_ms, kernel_choice_id, and batch_delay_ms.
[57:00] Sophie Chen: Recap — Diego shares profiler traces & kernel sweep, Sophie sends SOC2 + VPC doc, Jonah provisions 8xA100 in staging and runs bench, team sync early Jan. Any other blockers?
[57:20] Maya Patel: No blockers. One ask: keep the RTT measurement script — we want reproducible numbers.
[57:35] Diego Martinez: Yep will include.
[58:00] Priya Rao: Thanks everyone.
[58:05] Sophie Chen: Thanks all, we'll follow up via email with artifacts and the calendar for the pilot kickoff.
[58:20] Meeting ended
